catalog_quote: For the prediction of placement of phonetic stress or stresses in a word, syllable weight is obviously most important phonologically. There is also the effect of intonation contours on at least the pitch, especially the final syllable, as apparently all or most intonation contours are falling. There is one other factor complicating somewhat this otherwise relatively simple phonological picture, the morphological factor that there are disyllabic stems and the first syllable of such stems, open reduced CV, must also be stressed. Those are the only light syllables that are stressed. This is an important exception, however minor, to the phonological predictability of stress, otherwise only on heavy syllables. ... Where penult and final syllable are both heavy, there is a markedly lower pitch on the final, higher on the penult, so e.g. ch’i:/leh ‘raven’, di:/ya’ ‘salt’, te’/ya’ ‘salmon’, sa’…

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every span of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the heavy-syllable definition is verbatim on p.120 of the open ANLA file we hold Prosody > Stress), consistent with the record's locator; the prior verification had already corrected the page range. Deciding source: Krauss's comprehensive reference grammar (2017 draft, published 2024 by De Gruyter Mouton as A Grammar of Eyak, ~1200 pp.), i.e. the top item in Glottolog's list, written by the sole modern describer of the language. Krauss himself says stress is impressionistic with no instrumental study, ranks syllable weight first and treats stem-initial light-syllable stress as a minor morphological exception, so 'weight-hedged / weight-sensitive (tentative), unbounded, CVV+CVC heavy' follows from the text.
